transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, thank you. Um, well, it's a little hard to explain exactly where it started, but what really brings me in today is just this... this constant restless feeling I've been having. It’s like, um, like I’m wound way too tight all the time, and I just can't fully settle. You know that feeling when a wind-up toy is cranked just one turn past where it should be? That's exactly how my chest and my limbs feel all day. 

And it's really starting to frustrate me because it happens even when I’m supposed to be doing something completely calm. Like at work—I'm a retail buyer, so I have these incredibly long, drawn-out seasonal planning meetings where we're looking at vendor catalogs and spreadsheets for hours, and I'm supposed to be calmly sitting there, but I just can't settle into my chair. My body is just buzzing the whole time. 

And it's not just work, either! It happens when I'm at home trying to do things I actually enjoy, things that are literally designed to be relaxing. I'll set up my easel in the sunroom to do some painting, which I love, or I'll roll out my mat to do some yoga—and yoga is supposed to be the ultimate way to center yourself and find peace, right?—but even then, I'm just twitchy and restless. I can't sink into the poses or just let myself be still and focus on the canvas. It’s like my motor is always running, and I thought maybe, well, maybe at my age I should be able to just sit quietly through a meeting or a twenty-minute yoga routine without feeling like I need to jump out of my own skin, you know?
Do you find yourself having repetitive thoughts or urges to do specific things when you're feeling restless?

No, no, it's not like that. It's not a specific thought in my head telling me to do something, or like I have to touch a doorknob three times or anything like that. It's really just a physical sensation, you know? Like my body itself is just... humming. I don't have this urge to, like, check the stove or wash my hands or repeat words in my head. My sister actually has a little bit of that where she has to check her locks a certain number of times before she leaves the house, and it takes her forever to get out the door, which is a whole other story, but it's not like that for me at all. 

For me, it's just this generalized, vague need to move. It’s not directed at anything specific. I don't think, "Oh, I need to go organize the pantry right now" or "I have to tap my foot." It's just that my foot starts tapping on its own because the energy has to go somewhere. Or I'll just shift in my chair fifty times during a meeting, not because I'm thinking about shifting, but because sitting still physically feels uncomfortable. It's almost like if I don't move, the buzzing inside me is going to get louder and louder until I explode. But it's never a conscious thought or a specific urge to do a specific task. It's just this constant, low-level physical restlessness that never really goes away, no matter what I'm doing or how much I try to just tell my body to relax.
Is this restless feeling something that you experience all the time, or are there periods where it goes away?

Gosh, you know, I've never really stopped to measure it like that. I mean, is it all the time? I'm not entirely sure if it ever completely goes away, or if I just get so busy that I stop noticing it for a minute. Because my days are just packed, right? I wake up, I'm immediately running through my mental checklist for the seasonal buys, I'm getting my coffee, commuting in traffic—which is an absolute nightmare, let me tell you, just sitting in that car makes my legs want to detach themselves and run down the highway without me. 

But then, if I'm walking through the warehouse or actually physically moving around the showroom floor at work, maybe I don't feel it as much? Or maybe I do and it's just blending in with the fact that I'm already moving? I really couldn't say for sure. I haven't kept a journal or anything to track it. My husband, bless him, he always says I never have an off switch, even when we're just watching TV in the evenings. He'll point out that my foot is going a mile a minute or I'm rearranging the throw pillows for the fifth time. So maybe it doesn't go away? 

But I just can't say with absolute certainty if there's a specific hour or day where I'm completely at zero. It's hard to separate the feeling from just... living my life, I guess? I don't know if that makes sense or if that's what you're asking, but yeah, I just haven't really noticed a clear pattern of it ever just turning off. It's just sort of the background noise of my life, I suppose.
Do you have trouble falling asleep or staying asleep at night because of this restless feeling?

Sleep? Um, actually, no. You would think so, right? With all that buzzing and the motor running all day, you'd think I'd be tossing and turning all night, but honestly, sleep is the one thing that isn't really a problem. 

It’s almost like... well, like my body just completely runs out of gas. By the time I finally get into bed—which, to be fair, can be a little late sometimes because I'll be up wiping down the kitchen counters for the third time or answering a few last-minute vendor emails on my iPad while my husband is already dozing off—but by the time my head actually hits the pillow, I am just out cold. I think because I'm expending so much energy all day just trying to sit still in those endless meetings or pacing around the showroom, I just crash. My husband always jokes that I don't fall asleep, I just power down like a machine whose plug got pulled. 

And staying asleep... well, I sleep pretty soundly through the night, too. I mean, unless the dog wakes us up. We have a golden retriever, Buster, and he has this terrible habit of barking at absolutely nothing at three in the morning, like the wind or a shadow, which is a whole different kind of exhausting, let me tell you. But as far as my own body waking me up because I feel restless or twitchy? No, I haven't really noticed that happening. Once I'm finally asleep, the buzzing seems to just... stop, or at least I'm too knocked out to feel it. It's really just the waking hours where I have to actually sit and be present that drive me absolutely up the wall.
Do you often feel anxious or worried when you're experiencing this restless feeling?

Anxious? Worried? No, not really. I mean, I wouldn't call it anxiety. It's not like I'm sitting there tapping my foot because I'm worried about, you know, the quarterly margins or whether a shipment is going to be late. I mean, I do worry about those things—who wouldn't in my line of work? The supply chain issues lately have been just a total nightmare, and trying to get a straight answer out of our overseas vendors is like pulling teeth. I could spend hours just worrying about whether the fall collection is going to hit the floor on time. 

But the restlessness itself? That's not driven by worry. It's not like I'm having a panic attack or my heart is racing because I'm scared of something. It's really just... physical. Like my body is a car idling too high. It's just this need to move. I don't feel a sense of dread or like something bad is going to happen if I don't get up and walk around. It's more of a frustration, I guess? Like, I'm sitting in a meeting, and someone is droning on and on about the new inventory software—which, by the way, is supposed to make our lives easier but has actually just created ten extra steps for every purchase order—and I'm just sitting there, and my legs are practically vibrating, and I'm just thinking, "Please, please let this be over so I can stand up." 

So it's not anxiety, it's just... impatience with my own body, maybe? Or impatience with the situation that's forcing me to sit still. I don't have those racing, worried thoughts that go along with the physical feeling. It's just the physical feeling itself. Just that constant, annoying hum that makes me want to jump out of my skin, but not because I'm afraid, just because I have to *move*.
Do you feel irritable when you're experiencing this restless feeling?

Irritable? Um... well, maybe? I don't know if irritable is the right word, honestly. It's not like I'm snapping at people just because my foot is tapping. I mean, if someone is being completely incompetent, like last week when the warehouse manager lost an entire pallet of cashmere sweaters—a whole pallet, just vanished into thin air!—then yes, I'll get irritable, but that's just normal, right? Anyone would be annoyed by that. 

But just from the restless feeling itself? I don't think it makes me angry or cranky in general. It's more like... I just get really, really frustrated that I can't just get up and do what I need to do. Like if I'm stuck on a conference call that could have easily been an email, and I'm just sitting there, bouncing my leg, I might get a little short with people if they keep dragging the meeting out. But it's not the restlessness making me mad, it's the fact that I'm trapped there while my body is screaming at me to move. So, I guess... no? Not irritable from the feeling itself. Just annoyed by the situations where I'm forced to sit and deal with it.
Are there any specific events or activities that trigger or worsen your restless feeling?

Specific events? Um... no, not really. I wouldn't say anything *triggers* it, because that makes it sound like it goes away and comes back, you know? Like, oh, I drank too much coffee, or oh, I have a big presentation with the executives, so *now* I'm restless. But it's not like that at all. 

It’s just... always there. It’s really just my baseline setting. I mean, sure, it’s a lot more *noticeable* when I’m forced to sit still, like I was saying about those awful inventory meetings, but the meeting isn't actually triggering the feeling. The feeling is already there, I’m just not allowed to do anything about it in the meeting, so it builds up. 

Even when I'm doing something incredibly active, it's there. Like, twice a year I go to the big apparel markets for work, right? Usually Vegas or New York, and you are literally walking miles and miles every single day inside these massive convention centers. You're going from booth to booth, feeling fabrics, negotiating with suppliers, grabbing a quick overpriced salad on the go... it is completely non-stop. And even then, when I'm moving constantly, that motor inside me is still running. I'm just actually using the energy, so it doesn't feel as frustrating. I'm putting it to work. 

But if I have to stop? Like, say I have to stand in a massive line for a cab at the end of the day outside the Javits Center? Boom, instantly I'm tapping my foot, shifting my weight from side to side, checking my phone a hundred times, looking down the street to see if cars are moving. So the cab line didn't trigger the restlessness, and the trade show didn't trigger it... it's just me. It's just how my body operates all the time. So, no, I really can't think of any specific triggers. It’s just a constant companion, whether I'm at the office, at home, or anywhere else.
Do you notice if your restless feeling is worse at certain times of the day?

Certain times of the day? Um, honestly, no. It’s not really a morning thing or an evening thing. Like I was just saying, it’s really just my baseline. And honestly, that’s exactly what brings me in to see you. It’s this constant restless feeling, like I’m just wound way too tight, all the time. 

I mean, you’d think maybe it would peak right after my morning coffee or something, but it doesn't matter what time it is. I just can’t fully settle. It happens even when I’m supposed to be doing something incredibly low-key. Like, it's one thing if it's 10 AM and I’m supposed to be calmly sitting through a two-hour seasonal planning meeting—which, as you can probably guess by now, is its own kind of torture when they start projecting those endless budget spreadsheets. But it happens during my personal time, too. 

A couple of years ago, I took up painting, thinking it would be this great, zen outlet, right? Just me, a canvas, some watercolors, maybe a glass of wine in the evening. But even then, I’m shifting in my stool, tapping the brush against the easel, feeling like I need to get up and pace around the room every five minutes. Or yoga! My sister practically dragged me to this restorative yoga class last month. It's supposedly the most relaxing thing on the planet, and everyone is lying there on their little mats breathing deeply, and I’m just lying there feeling that exact same tight, wound-up hum. I couldn't settle into the poses at all. I was just mentally counting the ceiling tiles and twitching my toes, just agonizingly waiting for the instructor to say we could get up. 

So, morning, noon, night... it really doesn't make a difference. Whether I'm at work trying to focus on a meeting, or at home trying to paint, or in a yoga studio... I'm just always wound too tight to actually settle down.
Do you feel unhappy or depressed when you're experiencing this restless feeling?

Unhappy or depressed? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, it's frustrating, absolutely. Like I was saying about the yoga class, it's agonizing to be stuck somewhere when you can't move, but it's not a sadness thing. I'm not sitting there feeling down in the dumps or hopeless or anything like that. 

It’s more of a physical... urgency? Like, my brain and my body are just humming along at a hundred miles an hour, and the rest of the world is moving at a snail's pace. I'm actually a pretty upbeat person, generally speaking! I love my job, even with the lost cashmere pallets and the endless budget meetings. I love the fast pace of the fashion industry, I love the travel, I love putting together a whole seasonal collection. It's exciting! I get a real thrill out of it. 

So, no, the restlessness doesn't make me depressed. It just makes me feel like I need to be *doing* something. If anything, when I'm forced to sit still and that restless feeling builds up, I just feel... eager? Anxious to get moving again? But definitely not depressed. I don't cry about it, I don't feel empty. I just feel like a sports car stuck in neutral while someone is revving the engine. You know? Just... waiting for the light to turn green so I can go, go, go. So, yeah, definitely not unhappy in that sense. Just constantly ready for action, even when there's no action to be had.
Are you having trouble completing tasks or fulfilling responsibilities because of this restless feeling?

Trouble completing tasks? Well... I mean, I *complete* them. I have to! I'm a buyer, if I didn't complete my tasks we wouldn't have any inventory for the fall season, and that would be a disaster. But... I guess the *way* I complete them, or how I handle those responsibilities, is definitely causing some friction lately. 

Like, at work, because I have that constant urge to just go, go, go, I tend to rush through the tedious stuff. The paperwork, the data entry. So, for example, I'll be entering purchase orders—and these are huge orders, right? Hundreds of thousands of dollars in merchandise, multiple shipping windows, different freight terms—and I just want to get it done so I can move on to the next thing. Because I'm rushing and I can't sit still long enough to properly focus on the spreadsheet, I make these silly, careless mistakes. It's gotten to the point where my planning coordinator has to do all this extra review on my files. She's constantly having to issue corrected purchase orders because I transposed a SKU number or messed up a delivery date while I was racing through it. It drives her absolutely crazy, and I feel terrible about making extra work for her, but I just can't seem to slow down enough to double-check my own typing. 

And it’s not just at the office, either. It’s affecting my personal life, too, like my responsibilities at home. You know, being a present partner, being a good listener. Take family dinners, for instance. We really try to sit down together in the evenings, which is supposed to be this nice, relaxing bonding time, but... it usually just ends up being incredibly tense. Because I’m sitting there, and my internal engine is just revving, and someone will be telling a story about their day, and they’re just talking *so slowly*. I can see where the story is going, so I just jump in. I finish their sentences, or I just bulldoze right past them to make a comment. I don't do it to be mean or dismissive! I just literally cannot hold the words in, it's like a physical pressure. But, of course, it makes everyone else at the table feel totally talked over and unheard. My husband actually brought it up last week, how stressful dinner has become because I just dominate the conversation and won't let anyone else finish a thought. 

So, yeah... I guess the restlessness is definitely getting in the way of things. Even if I am technically still getting my job done, it's causing a lot of extra work at the office and a lot of tension at home.
Do you experience any difficulties with concentration or attention when you're feeling restless?

Concentration? Yes, exactly. That’s really what I was just getting at with those purchase orders. It’s like my attention span just... evaporates when that restless feeling kicks in. I’ll be at my desk—I actually got one of those standing desks recently, thinking maybe if I stand I can focus better, but honestly it doesn't really fix the attention part, it just lets me fidget on my feet instead of in a chair. 

But I'll be standing there, and I’ll have all the vendor files open on my dual monitors. And I swear to you, I really *think* I am paying attention. Over the past couple of years especially, it's become a real pattern. I’ll think I’ve checked a vendor spreadsheet incredibly carefully. I’ll go line by line, I'll tell myself, "Okay, you're focused, you're looking at the data." I’ll be so confident that it's perfect and ready to go. And then, sure enough, our planning coordinator catches the mistakes. 

Like I was saying before, she's having to review all my files now, and she'll point out that I transposed a SKU, or—and this just happened on a huge international order—I completely missed a freight surcharge that was clearly listed right there in the vendor terms, or I carried the totally wrong quantity into the final purchase order. 

Like, I'll look right at an order for 500 units of a seasonal knit, and somehow I type in 50. Or 5,000! Because my brain is just skipping ahead. It's like I'm looking at the details but my mind refuses to actually lock onto them because it's in such a hurry to move to the next thing. So I'm reading the numbers, but I'm not actually absorbing them. It is so incredibly frustrating to realize you spent twenty minutes staring at a spreadsheet, thinking you were being diligent, and you still managed to miss a massive freight surcharge just because your brain couldn't sit still long enough to process the fine print. So, yes, my concentration is definitely taking a huge hit.
Are your personal relationships being affected by your constant need to move and restlessness?

Oh, absolutely. I mean, I mentioned the dinners with my husband just a minute ago, right? That’s really just the tip of the iceberg, honestly. It definitely affects our relationship in other ways, especially when we have downtime. Or, well, what's *supposed* to be downtime. 

Take our weekends, for example. Saturday and Sunday are supposed to be the days you relax and unwind, maybe sit on the patio with a cup of coffee and just enjoy the morning. My husband loves doing that. But I just... I can't do it. I can't just sit there with him. Even on weekends, I tend to finish one thing and immediately start another, without even taking a breath. 

I’ll be up and moving, throwing a load of laundry in, and while the washer is filling, I’ll think, "Oh, let me just check my work emails real quick." Because I'm dealing with overseas vendors a lot, so there's always something sitting in my inbox. So I'm firing off emails, and then before I even close my laptop, I’m pulling out these product samples I brought home from the office—because I always bring work home, there's always a new fabric swatch or a seasonal color palette to review—and I'm completely reorganizing them all over the dining room table. And then, you know, I'll walk past a canvas in the hallway and decide I need to touch up a painting I started three months ago, so I'm getting the brushes out... 

It’s just this endless, continuous chain of tasks. I bounce from one thing to the next to the next. And my husband, bless his heart, he just looks at me and says I never really power down. He tells me it's exhausting for *him* just watching me buzz around the house all weekend. He'll ask me to just come sit on the couch and watch a movie, and I'll try, I really will, but ten minutes in I'm up again because I remembered the pantry needs reorganizing. So yes, it definitely creates this disconnect between us, because he wants a relaxing weekend with his wife, and I'm treating Saturday morning like a competitive sport. It's hard on him, I know it is.
Are there any hobbies or activities that you've had to stop or significantly reduce due to this restless feeling?

Stop them? Oh, gosh, no. No, honestly, it’s the exact opposite! I haven't had to stop or reduce anything at all. If anything, this restless feeling makes me take on *more* hobbies. It’s like I’m constantly looking for a new outlet for all this energy because I just can't sit still. 

Like, I mentioned that painting earlier... I still do that, but then a few months ago I decided I absolutely had to learn how to make my own ceramics. So I bought a beginner's pottery wheel and set it up in the garage, and then before I even really mastered centering the clay, I got completely obsessed with container gardening for the patio. Which, you know, my husband thought was a lovely, relaxing idea at first, until I came home with forty different terracotta pots and started frantically researching soil pH levels and companion planting at two in the morning. 

So, no, I don't drop things or stop doing them. I just kind of... hoard activities, I guess? I cram them all into my schedule. I have to have my hands busy constantly, whether I'm attempting to watch a movie or just hanging out at home. Now, I guess you could say I don't always *finish* the projects for these hobbies. Our spare room is basically a graveyard of half-knit sweaters, half-painted canvases, and bead-sorting trays that I swear I'm going to get back to eventually. I just cycle through them all at warp speed. The idea of reducing an activity just doesn't even compute for me, because I feel like I need all these different projects just to channel that constant buzzing feeling. So, yeah, I definitely haven't stopped or reduced any of my hobbies. I just keep adding to the pile!
Do you find yourself avoiding certain situations or activities because of this restless feeling?

Avoid things? Um, no, I really don't think I do. Actually, it’s funny you ask that, because you would think I *would* want to avoid things where I know I have to sit still, right? Like, in my line of work as a buyer, we have these massive seasonal line reviews. And I mean, they are *long*. We'll be stuck in this stuffy, windowless conference room on the fourth floor for literally four or five hours at a time, just going through next fall's outerwear catalog or looking at hundreds of different zipper options for fleece jackets or whatever the vendor brought in. It’s exactly the kind of situation where my brain and my body are just screaming to get out and move. 

But I don't avoid it. I can't, really, since it's my job, but even if I could, I don't think I would. I just... I bring the restlessness right in there with me. Instead of skipping the meeting or making an excuse to leave, I’ll just be the person who volunteers to stand by the whiteboard and write down the item numbers, or I'll get up to refill my coffee cup like six times, or I'll stand in the back and physically rearrange the sample garments on the rolling racks while the rep is still doing their PowerPoint presentation. 

And it’s the exact same in my personal life, too. Like, my husband loves the theater, and we have season tickets to the performing arts center downtown. Sitting through a two-and-a-half-hour play is honestly physical torture for me sometimes because I just want to stretch my legs and do something active. But I never tell him I won't go. I never avoid it. I just go, and I end up crossing and uncrossing my legs a hundred times, or folding and unfolding the playbill until it's practically origami, or digging around in my purse for a peppermint every fifteen minutes. I'm sure the people sitting next to us are completely annoyed by me, but... yeah, I don't avoid the situations themselves. I just sort of bulldoze my way into them and fidget my way through, because if I started avoiding every situation where I felt restless, I mean, I'd literally never do anything. I'd never go anywhere! So, no, I definitely don't avoid things. I just kind of show up and make everyone else deal with my pacing.

Has the way you've been feeling and acting due to this restlessness been relatively consistent over time, or have you noticed any significant changes or variations in how it affects your daily life and relationships?

Well, I mean, I’ve always been a busy bee, you know? Always on the go. But as far as it being exactly the same over time... no, actually, I would say there has definitely been a shift. It hasn't always been quite this intense. I’d say it has been noticeably harder to manage for... oh, let me think. It has been about two years and two months now. Yes, exactly that, because it was right around the time my husband's parents started having all these massive arguments with each other and the rest of the family. 

Ever since then, these in-law conflicts have just completely started taking over more of our evenings. And I mean really taking over. We used to come home from work, and even if I was puttering around the kitchen or sorting through my vendor catalogs, it was relatively peaceful. But for the last two years and a couple of months, it is just constant drama. His mother will call right when we are trying to eat, and she will just go on and on, and then my husband gets off the phone and he is so stressed, and he wants to vent about it. Which I understand, I really do! He needs a sounding board, and I want to be there for him. 

But having to sit there in the living room and listen to all this heavy, stressful family politics every single night... it just makes that buzzing feeling in my body go absolutely haywire. I can't just sit on the sofa and nod while he dissects whatever his dad said. I physically cannot do it. So that is when I really start tearing through the house, you know? I will start scrubbing the baseboards, or I will pull everything out of the hall closet to reorganize the winter coats, just to have an excuse to be moving while we talk about it. So, yeah, the restlessness itself isn't new, but how hard it is to actually rein it in and manage it? That has definitely spiked since all this in-law stuff started eating up our nights. It just adds this whole extra layer of nervous energy that I have to burn off somehow, and I just keep finding more things to clean or organize or rearrange while he talks!
Do you feel that your restlessness is ever linked to feeling overwhelmed or emotionally charged?

Overwhelmed? Um... you know, I really don't think so. I know I just said that thing about the in-law drama making it harder to manage, but it's not that I'm emotionally overwhelmed by their fighting, if that makes sense? Like, I'm not sitting there feeling all this heavy angst or getting upset myself. It's really just the fact that I'm trapped on the couch having to listen instead of doing something! 

Honestly, I don't really get overwhelmed very easily in general. In my line of work, you kind of can't. When you're a buyer, everything is a massive emergency to somebody. A shipment of cashmere-blend sweaters gets delayed at customs, or a vendor suddenly discontinues the exact dye lot you planned an entire holiday collection around... I mean, other people in the corporate office will be absolutely losing their minds, totally emotionally charged, practically crying in the breakroom. But I don't feel that way. I just pivot and handle it. 

But the restless feeling? That's just... always there, regardless of my mood. It doesn't matter if I'm dealing with a massive supply chain crisis at work or if I'm literally just sitting on my patio on a beautiful, breezy Saturday morning with absolutely nothing on my to-do list and not a single care in the world. I could be completely blissed out, totally relaxed in my mind, and my foot will still be tapping a mile a minute, or I'll suddenly feel this intense, overwhelming urge to get up and deadhead all the geraniums right that second. 

So, no, I really wouldn't tie it to my emotions at all. It's not like a nervous habit that only pops up when I'm stressed or upset. It's just my normal operating speed, I guess? Whether I'm happy, sad, bored, or whatever... the motor is just always running at the exact same speed. So, yeah, no, I haven't noticed it being linked to feeling overwhelmed at all. It's just my baseline.
Are you able to engage in quiet activities like reading a book without feeling the need to get up and do something else?

Um... quiet activities. Honestly, I'm not really sure, because I just don't even attempt them anymore! I mean, reading a book? I can't even tell you the last time I sat down with the intention of just quietly reading. 

Oh, wait, yes I can. Let me think, it was last summer. My husband and I rented this little A-frame cabin up near the lake for a long weekend, and it was supposed to be this totally unplugged, relaxing retreat. No Wi-Fi, no cell service, just nature. I brought this huge hardcover biography of a fashion icon that I’d been meaning to read for months. I got myself all set up on this beautiful screened-in porch, in a rocking chair, with a glass of iced tea. It was picture-perfect, right? The exact kind of quiet activity you're talking about. 

But I swear to you, I didn't make it through three pages before I felt this... this literal itch in my legs to get up. I just couldn't sit there. I told myself, "Oh, I'll just go inside and check if we brought enough paper towels for the weekend." So I got up, checked the pantry, ended up reorganizing the canned goods the host had left in there, wiped down the counters, swept the kitchen floor, and then finally went back to the book. I sat down, read maybe one more page, and then I got up again to see if the porch door squeaked, and I ended up trying to fix the hinge with a butter knife from the kitchen! 

So, I guess the answer is no, I definitely haven't noticed being able to just sit and do something quiet like that. My brain just immediately says, "Okay, what's next? What can we physically do? What needs fixing or moving?" Even if I try to force myself to just sit and do a crossword puzzle or something, I always end up standing up. I'll literally take the crossword puzzle and pace around the kitchen island with it, or I'll just abandon it completely to go deadhead the flowers or fold laundry. I just don't have a "quiet mode" in my system. It's like my body physically rejects the idea of just sitting still for leisure. So yeah, I don't really have any quiet hobbies at all because I just can't stick to them without popping up to do something else every five minutes.
Can you tell me about the last time you tried to watch a movie or TV show without getting up to do something else?

Oh, a movie? Gosh, let me think. Just this past Friday, actually! My husband really wanted to watch this new historical drama that just came out on streaming, the one everyone at his office has been talking about. He made a whole evening out of it—popped the good popcorn on the stove, not the microwave kind, dimmed all the lights, got us set up on the couch. And I really, genuinely wanted to watch it with him. I was interested in the story! But I think I made it maybe twenty, possibly twenty-five minutes before I just couldn't take it anymore. I told him I needed to go grab a sparkling water, and while I was in the kitchen, I started wiping down the countertops, and then I remembered an email I needed to send, and before I knew it, I was just watching the rest of the movie from the kitchen island while sorting through the mail. 

I just... I can't stay planted. It’s not just movies or TV shows, either. It’s literally any situation where I'm expected to be glued to a seat for an extended period of time. Like at work, for example. If a meeting runs long—and believe me, in my industry, vendor pitch meetings can drag on for absolute hours because they want to walk you through every single colorway of every single garment—I just cannot stay in my chair. I keep finding reasons to get up. I’ll stand up and say I need to look closer at the fabric samples on the back table, or I’ll volunteer to go get water for everyone, just to have an excuse to be on my feet. 

And it’s the exact same thing at home, especially with all that family drama I was telling you about earlier. If we’re having one of those really tense family dinners with my in-laws, oh my goodness, I am up and down like a yo-yo.
